div.p: The President of Mexico, Mr. Aleman, has transmitted to the United Nations a proposal which his Government has made in an effort to remove the remaining obstacle to an armistice in Korea.

The proposal of the Mexican Government takes account of the fact that agreement has been reached between the two sides in Korea on all of the provisions of an armistice with the exception of those articles dealing with prisoners of war. Even in this respect, as the Mexican Government has noted, there is a large measure of agreement. The Communists have declared that they were prepared to return to the United Nations 12,000 United Nations’ prisoners and representatives of the United Nations have frequently stated that we are prepared to return 83,000 prisoners of war whom we hold. The only outstanding issue in the armistice negotiations relates to persons not included in these numbers.

The Mexican Government has proposed that the prisoners of war each side has already offered to return to the other be immediately exchanged, and has suggested a way of dealing with the remaining outstanding
issue so that an armistice need not await the final disposition of this question.

This Government, and the other members of the United Nations with which it is associated are sincere in their desire to see an armistice completed in Korea. It is true, as the Mexican Government states, that a large area of agreement has now been established in the armistice negotiations.

As agent of the United Nations for the Unified Command in Korea, I therefore propose that the opposing sides mutually undertake to carry out all the articles that have been agreed to by the negotiators dealing with matters other than prisoners of war, and to take those actions which each side has already declared itself ready to take by way of returning prisoners of war to the control of the other side. This would mean that the United Nations would return 83,000 prisoners to Communist control; that the Communists would return 12,000 prisoners to United Nations control; that there then would be an immediate ceasefire and armistice in Korea; and that the persons not included in the numbers to be exchanged would be the subject of subsequent negotiations. The Mexican Government has suggested one possible basis for such negotiations. There are other ways in which this matter could be dealt with without the use of force. If the Communists share our desire to bring an end to fighting in Korea, the way is open.
